And they beat him wondering why did he need a candle. On Heder they found a needle, a sewing needle, and they beat him. So this is something that I witnessed myself. Whatever they found on people, whatever objects that could be used to cut was used as a pretext for beating.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how were the beatings carried out? With instruments or with just hands or kicks or what?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They beat them with cables, with chair legs, whatever they had on them. And if they had nothing on them, they would use their hands, because all of these men were very well developed and large -- or at least, that's how it seemed to me out of fear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you were beaten, because you'd been examined by the Red Cross, what was used to beat you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was beaten by hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, the beatings, were they carried out entirely by the guards or by others as well?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were not guards. The guards were outside of the camp. These were military policemen who - how shall I put it? - who were in charge of order in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know whether Lieutenant Colonel Popovic was ever present when these beatings were carried out?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you forced to work whilst you were at the camp?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not forced. I was beaten. But other people did go to work. They built a church; they dug out water canal; they had to clear some plants and some bushes; they had to go and load something in the forest -- wood.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know apart from that -- I'm sorry. Forget that. Did anybody that you recognised from the -- from either Sanski Most or Banja Luka, from politicians there, visit the camp whilst you were there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that in our stable a delegation came to visit and Andjelko Grahovac talked to us. He told us, "You people from Sanski Most will go home once Sanski Most is liberated from the Green Berets. The food will improve. There will be more food."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was he alone, or did somebody come with him?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were other people there whom I don't know, so I can't tell you who was there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want you to look, please, at a short film clip which I think you've seen, because you've got yourself, of Manjaca in August of 1992. And I then want you just to stop -- if you shout "stop," the audiovisual should hear it -- when we come to a point where you want to make a comment?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is yet again the Ashdown visit. And it's P468. Yes. If we could start the video -- can somebody -- is it on -- can somebody put it on in front of the witness, please - sorry - before we start. All right. Yes. If we could run the film. And then, Mr. Zulic, just shout "stop," if there's a point that you want to mention something.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The sound seems to have gone. It doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Right now you can see this container, jerrycan on the screen, and a man distributing water. This is how the water was distributed. So this rucksack, this backpack, was used for this row of people that you can see. Actually, there are two rows, to the left and to the right. So two inmates were charged with distributing water to everybody so that everybody would get about half a cup of water.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we run the film on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Stop. Here on my right side you can see me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you -- yes, I think you will have to --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the white shirt, T-shirt.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is that on the right-hand side roughly one -- about half a dozen men in?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Slightly --

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sixth or seventh person.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Slightly leaning forward.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Because I couldn't sit properly, so I had to lean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And can I just ask. Was this when you were inside the stable, did you all have to sit like that all the time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Somewhere until the end of August. And we had to bend our heads as well. But this occasion here was different because the television crew was there. So we were allowed to look to the side as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So normally you had to look down, did you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is how we had to look, down.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And while we're on that subject, if you had to speak to a guard did you have to adopt a particular position?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to bend our heads down and keep our hands on our bags. Actually, we weren't allowed to go out and talk to the guard at all. But if the guard called you or if you looked to the side, to the right or to the left, just a little bit, then the guard would call you and ask you why you did so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Could we just finish the clip, then. If you'd like to run on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we stop that. Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, do you remember the visit by this --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can stop the film completely. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you remember the visit by this politician?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bernard Kouchner, yes, I remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You remember the visit from Mr. Kouchner, do you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before any international people visited the camp, was there any sort of cleaning or tidying or any difference made in what the camp looked like?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had to clean the floor because that had to be prepared for the visit. We had to clean and straighten everything out. And if somebody had extra clothes, the clothes had to be put away so that they wouldn't be found hanging somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, finally, Mr. Zulic, you were released, as you've told us, on the 23rd of November. As a result of what happened to you, both in Betonirka and later in Manjaca, have you suffered any permanent injuries or disabilities or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Disabilities -- yes. I don't know to what a percentage this disability is, but this finger here is broken and I can't use it; however, I have to live with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You told us that when you were examined by the Red Cross, they said you had injuries to your chest and the like. Did you ever receive treatment for your ribs or anything of that nature, any other injuries, whilst you were in the camp?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't treated, but Dr. Meho Derviskadic, the doctor, brought me in secret some medication and he said if somebody saw me doing -- if somebody saw me bringing this, they would kill me. And this was vials for injections, for shots.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you -- do you still have residual effects of the injuries that were caused to your chest?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. I still have -- have to live with consequences. I can't walk about a lot. And if before the weather changes, it is very difficult for me to walk and to move around.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in respect of your teeth, which you told us about, that were knocked out by the pistol, in fact did you have to have replacement teeth?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Zulic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Do you need --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Cayley will be here if any cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you certainly can. Thank you. Now, Mr. Zulic, I have to explain to you something very briefly. The Prosecution has finished with its series of questions that it had prepared for you; however, you now need, according to our Rules of Procedure, to be questioned, examined, by the Defence teams. That's a right of cross-examination, that each and every accused person here has. I don't know who is going to go first.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You are going first to be cross-examined by the Defence team for General Talic. And Madam Fauveau will be conducting the cross-examination. Thank you. Madam Fauveau, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you spoke about checkpoints that were established at the end of 1991. Could you please be more specific and tell us who manned those checkpoints at the end of 1991.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police was at those checkpoints, a mixed military police. There were Serbs and Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which unit those military policemen -- mixed military policemen belonged to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Until when was the military police mixed ethnically?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until about the end of March, beginning of April.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know which unit the Serb military police belonged to that remained after that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I think they belonged to the 6th Krajina Brigade. I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you know that they were military policemen?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know because in those days, it was only the military police that wore camouflage uniforms and white belts.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know the people who were at those checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can. Hajrulah Lokic, then Mile Tucak from Podlug, as far as I know. But of course I didn't know all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were these men at the checkpoints also before March 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were the men who were there before March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And did they stay on after March 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know the people who were at the checkpoint after March 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know some of them but not many, because there were many checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us the names of the people you knew?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two brothers from Todorovica Sokak, Zeljko and -- I know the other brother too, but they were probably as close to the checkpoint -- but just now I can't remember the name. So if I may, when I remember I'll tell you the name of the other brother. Both of them used to work with me at the mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these people that you just mentioned, were they at the checkpoints also before March?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were before March. Tucak and Lokic did not stay on, but these ones did.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you know whether these people belonged to the 6th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you cannot assert, regarding the others either, that they belonged to the 6th Brigade. That is right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't, because I didn't ask them who they belonged to and they didn't tell me either.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about Muslim patrols that were organised in your village. Until when did those patrols exist?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those patrols existed -- first of all, they were not so well organised. But until about the 25th of 26th of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the 7th of June, page 6854 of the French transcript you spoke about the attack on the municipality building in Sanski Most, and you said that this was in May 1992. Can you confirm that statement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The attack on the municipality building -- will you please repeat the question for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that the attack on the municipality building in Sanski Most took place in May 1992. Do you confirm that statement?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying that I don't remember the exact date, whether it was the end of April, the beginning of May when the municipality building was attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In your written statement of 2001 you spoke about the attack on the police station in Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask the usher to show the witness his statement from 2001 in Serbo-Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In that statement - it is on page 5 of the English version, the second paragraph if we look from the bottom of the page, and in the Serbo-Croat version it's the third from the top - you said that the Muslim police station in Sanski Most was attacked on the 14th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here on the 27th of May, 1992 the regular army and the reservists gathered the population of Mahala in the soccer field --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I'm talking about the 14th of May, page 5, third paragraph from the top.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me. This is correct that that is what I said to the investigator.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm today that on the 14th of May, 1992 there was an attack against the Muslim police station?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then and now I am claiming that. That is what I told the investigator, that I cannot remember exactly five to ten days accuracy because I didn't have those books on me that I have now, which means that I can be wrong by a certain number of days. Whether it was the 14th of May or maybe the 24th of May, I really don't know, so I can't confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why, then, in that case didn't you say that you don't know the date?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told the investigator that I think it was like that. I said at the end of the interview that all the dates listed may not be absolutely accurate. One, two, or five days -- I may be wrong ten years later.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But why didn't you say that you don't know the date?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the end I said that it's not that I don't know but I simply cannot assert with certainty -- if I had this diary on me, then I would know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So what is written in this statement does not correspond to what you said; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, Madam Fauveau, because he has already answered that question. He has said already that this is what he told the investigator, but what he told the investigator may not be accurate as regards the date I itself. So he's answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: On 7 June, page 6877 of the French transcript, you spoke of an attack on the village of Cirkici. Could you tell us when that attack took place?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, can I -- may I ask you to repeat the name of the village, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Cirkici village. The village -- spoke about that on the 7th of June, on page 68 to 77 [As interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It says the 2nd of June, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it was the 2nd of June, according to your recollection or is it according to your notebook?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the basis of my notes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And during that attack on Cirkici, where were you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was at home.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were in your own house, in your own village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: What is the distance between your village and the village of Cirkici?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 10 kilometres, 10 to 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How could you see what was happening at Cirkici?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see anything. I didn't say I saw anything. I didn't write that down. But refugees arrived, that's one thing. And secondly, Radio Sana makes an announcement saying that Green Berets had appeared in Cirkici, and that was for us a sign that the village had been attacked.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you personally could not see what was happening at Cirkici could you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I told you I didn't write that down either. When the refugees came, they said that the village had been burnt. Unfortunately after the war, what the refugees had told us proved to be true.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you personally didn't know whether there were any Green Berets at Cirkici?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also spoke about an attack on Skuceni Vakuf. It is on the same page, 6877 of the transcript of the 7th of June. Yes. Did you see that attack?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you don't know exactly what happened at Skuceni Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know but whey heard from refugees. I didn't write down what had happened. The refugees said, "The village is burning and we are fleeing." "What happened?" And they said, "They attacked."

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't know whether there were any fighting at Skuceni Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether there was any combat. But as there were no wounded Serb soldiers, it was clear that there was no battle.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: How did you know that there were no wounded Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because they would have reported it on the radio, so many Serb soldiers wounded. All I had to do was to listen to the radio and to know what was happening, and I had to listen to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But this radio also spoke about the Green Berets, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So that information too could have been correct.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it could never be correct. Where would the Green Berets appear from in 20 households?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why, in that case, did you believe that information regarding no Serb soldiers being wounded?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because even if a single soldier had been wounded, they would have announced it on Radio Sana. When Vrhpolje was attacked and when there was fighting, they immediately reported how many soldiers had been killed and they immediately reported that they would take their revenge; therefore, that was a sign and logic told you that you should believe the refugees that were coming from there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, you also believed in the reports you heard on the radio. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accuracy of the radio reports? I believe them, but I always turned them upside down, that is, the opposite.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the hearing on the 7th of June, page 6861, you said that the inhabitants of Mahala were asked to leave their houses; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So it was the Serb who demanded the inhabitants of Mahala to leave their houses?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So the Serbs didn't wish the inhabitants of Mahala to be wounded or killed during combat; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which combat?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: The fighting in Mahala.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Mahala, as far as I know, there was no fighting. No one put up any resistance to the Serbs in Mahala, as far as I know. But I have to quote something now and tell you on the basis of the Serb Radio Sanski Most. As far as I can remember, actually, Miso, a reporter, was covering the fighting in Mahala as if it was a football match. "The Serb forces are attacking," he said. And then he says, "And the Green Berets are responding." There's no logic there. How can a reporter be standing -- unfortunately I had that tape, but it's been destroyed. Your Honours, you would be able to see what it was about, because it was a radio -- a tape from the radio.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for you to stop for a break, just let me -- preferably within the next five minutes. Whenever it's -- just please yourself, suit yourself, and tell me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you wish, we can have the break now, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll have a break of 20 minutes, resuming at quarter to 6.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we spoke about Mahala, about a journalist from the Serb radio who reported about what was going on in Mahala. And at that point you said that the journalist could not have seen, could not have been there. Where were you yourself while these events were taking place in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Podbrijezje listening to the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore you personally didn't see what was going on in Mahala?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that some people who were handicapped, could not move, remained in Mahala and were killed. Why did these people remain in Mahala? If you know, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know. They remained there because they were handicapped and they didn't have enough time to leave Mahala. It was reported at 9.00 or around 9.00 -- or rather, I apologise -- it was reported, I think, at 4.00 that -- it was announced that all civilians had to leave Sabica canyon -- to come out from Muhici and Mahala to the range and go to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So therefore the members of the family of those handicapped people in fact deserted them, left them in the house.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't leave them. My father-in-law was not left by my mother-in-law. She went out to take the neighbour from the house next door to her own house; however, a shell fell on the house and set it on fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So your father-in-law was killed during the shelling; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not killed. He was set on fire. He burnt in the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But a shell fell on the house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody came with the intention to set the house on fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That day -- or rather, that night -- no, the house was not set on fire. Nobody set out to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us, still on the 7th June, page 6877, that the refugees were in your village; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Q. You said then that the army forced them out. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. First they were sent to Jajce on the 1st of June, yes, 1st of June. That's right. They were deported to Jajce. So first they were called to come out on the radio, and then they boarded them into buses and sent to Jajce. And then later on a part -- one group of refugees was sent to Majdan and the other one was left in Podbrijezje. And the second time when they announced this on the radio, the refugees refused to leave because they knew that there would be a problem. However, the army came, they blocked the village of Podbrijezje and brought in the buses from Kamengrad and they went door to door and collected refugees. That day was Bajram, the greatest Muslim holiday.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what date it was. Do you know the date?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 14th of June, 1992. It was Bajram. You can verify this. And you'll see that it was Bajram, Hajji Bajram [phoen]. This is the day when sheep are slaughtered and the meat is distributed and the refugees could not celebrate it on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us that members of that army had a star; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was that a red star?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You also told us that it was the regular army. Can you tell us what regular army -- which regular army had a star as their insignia on the 14th of June, 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The JNA.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it true that on the 14th of June the JNA was not present in Bosnia any more?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I don't know that the JNA was not present in Bosnia. However, I know that in Manjaca on July 7th I saw trucks with the JNA insignia. And if it wasn't the JNA army then how come these trucks had JNA signs on them in Manjaca on the 7th of July?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: According to you, how long did the JNA stay in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in May 1992 a regular army of the Republika Srpska was created?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So therefore you don't know that the regular Serb army did not have a red star on its uniform after that.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. You just told me that the army of Republika Srpska was created. Are you asking me something else now?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you know that the Army of Republika Srpska did not have a red star.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. While I was free, there were people wearing cockades. We called them Seselj's people. The White Eagles. They had a white ribbon. And then there were also members of 6th Krajina Brigade and then there were also some private troops, as they called them, and the SOS. And what the SOS is, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And were you able to determine every time -- each time to which of these armies a soldier belonged?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't to determine that each time. We knew to whom these people with cockades belonged. The members of the SOS wore white ribbons -- not white ribbons but camouflage ribbons around their head. They also had rifles. Medeni had one of them; Tripkovic did as well. I saw them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please describe for us the uniforms worn by the SOS members.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were camouflage uniforms. The three people that I just mentioned to you drove around in a red Lada car.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I continue or not, because I think that the Prosecutor wanted 20 minutes at the end of the session today and then the Defence needs a few more minutes. So I don't know, shall we continue cross-examining or should we now switch is return to administrative issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't think I'm going to take 20 minutes, to be honest with you. I mean, Mr. Ackerman may have some points. I think I may take about five minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, Madam Fauveau. I will tell you when to stop.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You told us just now that the members of the SOS had camouflage uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These three people that I saw. That's right. I didn't see all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please take a look at your statement from 2001. On page 3 -- I don't know if you still have the statement in front of you.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 3, both in the English and B/C/S version, in the last paragraph. You spoke about members of various units, and you stated that members of the SOS wore olive-grey uniforms. These uniforms that you mentioned in this statement of yours, they were not camouflage uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's what it says here. However, I know that these three men wore camouflage uniforms. Njunja, Medeni, and Tripkovic, those three. Whereas the rest, they probably had these other olive-grey uniforms. These in fact were uniforms that were confiscated from the Muslims, from those that were in the Territorial Defence before the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, some members of the SOS had camouflage uniforms and the others had olive-grey uniforms; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At the hearing on June 7th, transcript page 6883 in French, you said -- you described one of the rooms in Betonirka in which you were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you stated that the room was not aired sufficiently because one of the windows that existed there was blocked, it was -- there was some kind of a concrete block blocking it. You confirm that today; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at page 9 of your statement given in 2001. In the English version, that's in paragraph 3 from the bottom of the page. And in the Serbo-Croatian version, it's the first paragraph on page 9. You said -- you said in this paragraph: [In English] "I heard people being beaten because the windows were open, and I could hear screams, moaning, and cries."

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I repeated today that a pallet of concrete blocks was placed on the window. I hope it was translated well. I didn't say it was a concrete block but a pallet of concrete blocks. I don't know if you know what it is. It is something that is put against the window some 20 to 30 centimetres from the window so that we couldn't go out through the window. I think that that's what I said today.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So therefore you remain by the statement given previously that the windows were open.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were no windows. But there was a pallet of concrete blocks against the window so that -- so there was no air coming in, and this is what I'm claiming.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: And why, then, did you state in 2001 to the Prosecution that the windows were open?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true that I said that they were open. I don't know. Maybe there was a problem with translation, because I didn't read this first statement. Perhaps it was a translating error. This is what I stand by. There were no window frames. There was just a pallet of concrete blocks stacked, a pile stacked, and they were brought there with a forklift to this concrete garage. And you know very well how the sound is carried in the night.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So what you stated back then in your statement, what is contained here in your statement does not correspond entirely to what you stated.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, now you told me that this was a concrete block, slab. I don't know exactly how to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in that statement that is before you, it says that the windows were open. This is what it says on page 9, paragraph 1, second line.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no window. They were practically open. There were no window frames. There were just concrete slabs in that place. So that means that they were not -- there was some space left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No more questions on this particular topic, Madam Fauveau, please, because I think the witness has explained himself already well enough what he meant and how he may have been mistranslated.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you came to The Hague, were you given an opportunity to read your statement again?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not this one but the other one, yes. There apparently are some technical errors in it, which I corrected.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: So you haven't seen this statement.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were arrested by four persons, all of whom were policemen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was a driver. He was not wearing a uniform, and the others were.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: At Betonirka the guards were also policemen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they weren't. Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who were the guards at Betonirka?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know to which unit they belonged?

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: But you are confident about those four who arrested you that they were policemen.

utterances.speaker: AHMET ZULIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for you, we can stop.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Whenever it's convenient for you, we can stop. But if you still have a few questions on this particular topic, you can finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I would like now to go to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Zulic, we need to stop here today. We will continue tomorrow and I would suppose -- can I anticipate that we will finish with this witness tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that I will finish tomorrow. But it is rather difficult for me to determine the amount of time that I will need.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will ask the witness a few questions, but briefly. Some 15 minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So hopefully tomorrow will be your last day here. You need to come again tomorrow at 2.15 and we will take it up from there. I thank you, Mr. Zulic, and you are now going to be escorted out of the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The first matter is we are now in possession of what we believe to be Mr. Rasula's diary, the original version of it. And I have a immediate suggestion to solve the problems that we are having with that document: That the Defence inspect it under our supervision -- we also have, I think -- I might not be correct on this -- but I think well over 100 documents -- originally documents apparently signed by Mr. Rasula. So we have other samples of his writing. I would suggest the Defence inspect it, the diary and the other documents, and if it is still questioned the next step - which is a very expensive step and one which, quite frankly, I think we should only take if there is some very good foundation to still assert that this document is a forgery - would be to send it to the home office laboratories in London for a question document examiner to examine the diary and the documents apparently signed by him in order to at least say whether those documents were both written by the same person. I mean, obviously they can't say whether or not it's Mr. Rasula --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's come to the second of these two suggestions you are making if and when it is necessary to come to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, with -- let's stop on the first one. Are there any comments on the proposition that is being made by Mr. Cayley to the Defence teams to inspect this -- what is allegedly the original diary of Mr. Rasula, and then we'll take it up from there depending on what the outcome of your inspection, if there will be one, will be, or do you require time until, say, tomorrow to think about it and then come back with a reply?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In any event, we would like to see that document, but I would like to specify that the document that we read before was in fact a false document. But that poses another question. For many of the documents this problem will arise because obviously somebody from inside the Tribunal added words on a document which was a copy of the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think Mr. Cayley's suggestion is -- is appropriate, that we have an opportunity to inspect it. And I don't think we can really go much beyond --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the time being, that's why I stopped him, actually, because I think it would be preempting several other issues and matters. First they inspect it, and then we see. Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: See what happens next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. That's my suggestion to you. Okay. So you will make arrangements -- I would imagine that this is taken up between the Prosecution and the Defence without the Trial Chamber having anything to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We can arrange a convenient time for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then come back to us when you are ready and you are in a position to enlighten us further.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: And the next -- and the final matter, is actually, on the order of witnesses. It's a slight change, only that two witnesses have essentially fallen away for the moment and simply because the witnesses that were planned for Thursday and Friday of this week are for us fixed points in time. They have to testify on those days. So Witness 7.12 will testify after this witness. And then Witness 7.139, 7.143, and 7.52. Witness 7.13 will go back to next week. And as I say, the only reason we've made that change is because we have to get those three witnesses in at the end of this week, beginning of next week. That's 7.139, 7.143, and 7.52.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Does that cause any problems to any of the Defence teams?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, it's the issue that I wanted to discuss. And I -- in direct response to your question, no, it doesn't cause any problems other than it re-establishes confusion as to where we go next. We had a list which we were told was the final list for Sanski Most, and then all of a sudden it's changed again. So I don't know where we're going after this week. It's pretty clear to me where we're going this week. But after that, I don't know whether we revert back to the old list or what we're going to do. And so I would hope the Prosecutor can get that cleared up for us fairly soon. The other thing, Your Honour, that concerns me - and I've discussed this with Mr. Cayley and Ms. Korner earlier today - I had first understood, and it turned out that I was wrong, that Witness 7.52 was only going to be able to be with us for one day and there was no way we were going to be able to complete all the examination and cross-examination of that witness in one day. I'm now told that he can also be available for our Trial Chamber on Monday. And maybe that will be enough and maybe it won't. I don't know. He's -- he's got quite an extensive bit of paperwork surrounding his proposed testimony. And it's likely that we would take more than two days with him. What I would -- what I would suggest to Your Honours, is that it somehow be made clear -- and this is for our witness as well as the Prosecutor's witnesses -- that once a witness comes here and sits in that chair and takes the oath, they're here until they're excused by the Court -- by the Chamber. And it's -- it -- we would work around their schedules as best we can and try to accommodate them as best we can but we can't have a situation where at the, you know, end of the direct the Prosecutor announces that the witness must leave in one hour and can't come back and therefore you have to do your cross in one hour. And I think that needs to be clearly understood, that once the witness is here the witness is here until the Chamber is satisfied that cross-examination has been appropriately allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cayley.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: I mean, in principle Mr. Ackerman is absolutely right. I mean, I can't disagree with what he's saying. In respect --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm glad you concede that.

utterances.speaker: MR. CAYLEY
utterances.text: In respect of this witness, the reason why we are somewhat sympathetic towards him is because he's testified a number of times at the Tribunal. He's a very busy man. He travels all over Europe and has a lot of business interest that he needs to attend to. But I think -- he's a form British army officer and I think he will understand that once the Chamber says, "Sorry, witness, but you are going to have to stay until you're finished," he will accept that position and stay. He did ask that he testify this coming Friday for reasons of his own calendar which we are trying to accommodate. But as Mr. Ackerman discussed with Ms. Korner, he will be available at least to this Chamber on Friday and Monday, and I think there will be an understanding that if it has to go on after that, it will. But he's supposed to be testifying in another case and we're trying to coordinate to get him in there as well. But that's the position with this witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you happy with that, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Any further points that you would like to raise? So I think we can call it a day. Well, I thank you, and we'll resume tomorrow in Courtroom I. Tomorrow will be Courtroom I. And then I think Friday we will be back in Courtroom II, here, in this fantastic courtroom. I thank you. Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: at 6.24 p.m., to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 18th day of June, 2002, at 2.15 p.m.
